explanation: The optic nerve (CN II) passes through the optic canal, carrying visual information from the retina to the lateral geniculate body, making it functionally part of the CNS rather than a true peripheral nerve.
keyConcept: Optic nerve (CN II) traverses the optic canal.

explanation: The oculomotor nerve (CN III) emerges in the interpeduncular fossa, anterior to the crossing of the tentorium margins, before dividing into superior and inferior branches that enter the orbit.
keyConcept: Oculomotor nerve emerges anterior to tentorium crossing.

explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is unique as the only cranial nerve to exit posteriorly from the dorsal midbrain, crossing at the superior medullary velum at the tentorium margin level.
keyConcept: Trochlear nerve exits posteriorly at tentorium crossing level.

explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) passes through the hypoglossal canal, which lies above the foramen magnum, carrying motor fibers to all intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles.
keyConcept: Hypoglossal nerve passes through hypoglossal canal above foramen magnum.

explanation: The cerebral part of the internal carotid artery gives five branches: ophthalmic, posterior communicating, anterior choroidal, anterior cerebral, and middle cerebral arteries, supplying the orbit, diencephalon, and cerebral hemispheres.
keyConcept: ICA cerebral branches: ophthalmic, posterior communicating, anterior choroidal, ACA, MCA.

explanation: The temporal fossa is bounded superiorly by the superior temporal line and inferiorly by the zygomatic arch, with the deep temporal fascia separating it from the temporalis muscle.
keyConcept: Temporal fossa: superior temporal line above, zygomatic arch below.

explanation: The infratemporal fossa is bounded laterally by the mandibular ramus, medially by the lateral pterygoid plate, anteriorly by the posterior maxilla, posteriorly by the styloid process, and superiorly by the greater wing of sphenoid.
keyConcept: Infratemporal fossa boundaries: mandible laterally, pterygoid plate medially, maxilla anteriorly, styloid posteriorly.

explanation: The infratemporal fossa communicates superiorly with the middle cranial fossa via foramen ovale and spinosum, anteriorly with the orbit via inferior orbital fissure, medially with the pterygopalatine fossa via pterygomaxillary fissure, and with the temporal fossa deep to the zygomatic arch.
keyConcept: Infratemporal fossa communicates: middle cranial fossa, orbit, pterygopalatine fossa, temporal fossa.

explanation: All muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoid) are innervated by the anterior division of the mandibular nerve (V3), except the medial pterygoid which receives a branch from the trunk.
keyConcept: Muscles of mastication: all by anterior division of V3 except medial pterygoid (trunk).

explanation: The muscles of mastication produce protrusion (lateral pterygoid, medial pterygoid, masseter) except temporalis which retracts; elevation is produced by all except lateral pterygoid which depresses; medial and lateral pterygoid together produce side-to-side grinding movements.
keyConcept: Mastication actions: protrusion (except temporalis), elevation (except lateral pterygoid), side-to-side movement.

explanation: Structures lateral to the lateral pterygoid include the ramus of mandible, superficial head of medial pterygoid, tendon of temporalis, maxillary artery, and pterygoid venous plexus.
keyConcept: Lateral relations of lateral pterygoid: mandible, medial pterygoid, temporalis tendon, maxillary artery, pterygoid plexus.

explanation: Medial to the lateral pterygoid lie the deep head of medial pterygoid, tensor palati muscle, middle meningeal artery, maxillary artery, mandibular nerve trunk, otic ganglion, and sphenomandibular ligament.
keyConcept: Medial relations of lateral pterygoid: medial pterygoid, tensor palati, MMA, V3 trunk, otic ganglion.

explanation: The three ligaments associated with the TMJ are the lateral ligament (thickening of joint capsule), stylomandibular ligament (from styloid to mandible), and sphenomandibular ligament (from spine to lingula).
keyConcept: TMJ ligaments: lateral, stylomandibular, sphenomandibular.

explanation: The posterior division of the mandibular nerve gives three branches: auriculotemporal (sensory to temple and ear), lingual (sensory to anterior two-thirds of tongue), and inferior alveolar (sensory to lower teeth and chin).
keyConcept: Posterior V3 branches: auriculotemporal, lingual, inferior alveolar.

explanation: The inferior alveolar nerve gives off the mylohyoid branch before entering the mandibular foramen, then continues as the mental nerve (exiting mental foramen) and incisive nerve (supplying lower anterior teeth).
keyConcept: Inferior alveolar branches: mylohyoid, mental, incisive nerves.

explanation: The maxillary nerve (V2) gives off a meningeal branch, two ganglionic branches to the pterygopalatine ganglion, the zygomatic nerve, and the posterior superior alveolar nerve.
keyConcept: Maxillary nerve branches: meningeal, two ganglionic, zygomatic, posterior superior alveolar.

explanation: The pterygopalatine fossa is bounded anteriorly by the posterior maxilla, posteriorly by the pterygoid process, medially by the palatine bone, and laterally it opens into the infratemporal fossa.
keyConcept: Pterygopalatine fossa: maxilla anterior, pterygoid posterior, palatine medial, open laterally.

explanation: The pterygopalatine fossa contains the third part of the maxillary artery, branches of the maxillary nerve, and the pterygopalatine ganglion with associated autonomic connections.
keyConcept: Pterygopalatine fossa contents: maxillary artery part 3, maxillary nerve, pterygopalatine ganglion.

explanation: The third (pterygopalatine) part of the maxillary artery gives posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, greater and lesser palatine, sphenopalatine, pharyngeal branches, and the artery of the pterygoid canal.
keyConcept: Third maxillary artery: posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, palatine, sphenopalatine, pharyngeal, pterygoid canal.

explanation: The pterygoid venous plexus drains into the maxillary vein, which then joins the superficial temporal vein to form the retromandibular vein, ultimately connecting to the external jugular system.
keyConcept: Pterygoid plexus drains to maxillary vein.

explanation: The pterygoid plexus communicates with the facial vein via the deep facial vein, with the cavernous sinus via emissary veins through foramen ovale and spinosum, and with the inferior ophthalmic vein.
keyConcept: Pterygoid plexus: facial vein, cavernous sinus, inferior ophthalmic vein connections.

explanation: The otic ganglion sits below the foramen ovale; its parasympathetic root comes from the inferior salivatory nucleus via tympanic branch of CN IX, tympanic plexus, and lesser petrosal nerve; it distributes to the parotid gland.
keyConcept: Otic ganglion: below foramen ovale; parasympathetic from inferior salivatory nucleus via tympanic plexus to parotid.

explanation: Sympathetic roots differ by ganglion: otic ganglion receives fibers around the middle meningeal artery, submandibular ganglion around the facial artery, and sphenopalatine ganglion around the internal carotid artery via the deep petrosal nerve.
keyConcept: Sympathetic roots: otic (MMA), submandibular (facial artery), sphenopalatine (ICA/deep petrosal).

explanation: The external jugular vein receives tributaries including the anterior jugular, transverse cervical, suprascapular, and posterior external jugular veins, draining superficial structures of the head and neck.
keyConcept: EJV tributaries: anterior jugular, transverse cervical, suprascapular, posterior external jugular.

explanation: The floor of the posterior triangle is formed by the semispinalis capitis, splenius capitis, levator scapulae, scalenus medius, and scalenus anterior muscles, from superficial to deep.
keyConcept: Posterior triangle floor: semispinalis capitis, splenius capitis, levator scapulae, scalenus medius and anterior.

explanation: Five important contents of the posterior triangle are the spinal accessory nerve, roots and trunks of the brachial plexus, cutaneous nerves of the cervical plexus, subclavian vein, and external jugular vein.
keyConcept: Posterior triangle contents: spinal accessory, brachial plexus roots/trunks, cervical plexus cutaneous, subclavian vein, EJV.

explanation: The cervical plexus cutaneous branches are the great auricular (C2-3 to ear and parotid), lesser occipital (C2 to lateral scalp), transverse cervical (C2-3 to lateral neck), and supraclavicular nerves (C3-4 to shoulder and chest).
keyConcept: Cervical plexus: great auricular, lesser occipital, transverse cervical, supraclavicular nerves.

explanation: The anterior triangle is bounded anteriorly by the anterior median line of the neck, posteriorly by the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid, and superiorly by the inferior border of the mandible and line extending to the mastoid process.
keyConcept: Anterior triangle: midline anterior, sternomastoid posterior, mandible/mastoid line superior.

explanation: The submental triangle has its apex at the symphysis menti, sides formed by the anterior bellies of the digastric muscles, base along the body of hyoid, and floor formed by the mylohyoid muscles.
keyConcept: Submental triangle: apex symphysis menti, sides anterior bellies of digastric, base hyoid body, floor mylohyoid.

explanation: Contents of the submental triangle include the submental lymph nodes, submental artery and vein, mylohyoid nerve and vessels, and small veins that contribute to the anterior jugular vein formation.
keyConcept: Submental contents: submental nodes, vessels, mylohyoid nerve and vessels, veins to anterior jugular.

explanation: The digastric triangle boundaries are: anterior belly of digastric, posterior belly of digastric with stylohyoid, and the inferior border of mandible to mastoid; the floor is formed by mylohyoid and hyoglossus.
keyConcept: Digastric triangle: anterior/posterior bellies of digastric, mandible to mastoid; floor mylohyoid and hyoglossus.

explanation: Five contents of the digastric triangle are the submandibular gland, submandibular lymph nodes, submandibular ganglion (parasympathetic), facial artery, and facial vein.
keyConcept: Digastric triangle contents: submandibular gland, LN, ganglion, facial artery and vein.

explanation: The carotid triangle is bounded superiorly by the posterior belly of digastric, anteriorly by the superior belly of omohyoid, posteriorly by the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid; the floor is formed by hyoglossus, thyrohyoid, and the middle and inferior pharyngeal constrictors.
keyConcept: Carotid triangle: posterior digastric superior, omohyoid anterior, SCM posterior; floor hyoglossus and constrictors.

explanation: The carotid triangle contains the common carotid artery and its bifurcation into the internal and external carotid arteries, along with the carotid body (chemoreceptor) and carotid sinus (baroreceptor).
keyConcept: Carotid triangle contains: CCA, ICA, ECA, carotid body and sinus.

explanation: The muscular triangle contains the infrahyoid (strap) muscles: sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, and omohyoid, which stabilize the larynx and hyoid during swallowing and speech.
keyConcept: Muscular triangle contains infrahyoid strap muscles.
